title: The Laramie Project
author: Moisés Kaufman and Members of the Tectonic Theater Project
target_audience: Students and educators studying contemporary American history
Readers interested in social justice and community responses to tragedy
General audiences seeking insight into hate crimes and their impact
core_themes: Homophobia and hate crimes in America
primary_purpose: To document and dramatize the aftermath of the 1998 hate crime murder of Matthew Shepard in Laramie, Wyoming, exploring how a community responds to violence motivated by bigotry and examining the broader social and cultural context of anti-LGBTQ+ prejudice in the United States.

structure_format.narrative_style: Verbatim theater using actual interviews, journal entries, and news reports
structure_format.organization: Divided into three acts, scenes constructed from over 200 interviews with Laramie residents and other relevant individuals
features: Minimalist stage directions allowing for flexible performance

key_concepts_lessons: Hate crimes have deep and lasting effects not only on victims and their families, but entire communities.
Diversity of responses emerges in the wake of tragedy—ranging from denial and anger, to empathy and activism.
Bearing witness and sharing stories is a crucial part of confronting and understanding prejudice.
Media coverage both reflects and shapes public attitudes toward marginalized groups.
Personal and collective healing after trauma requires honesty, dialogue, and reflection.
notable_features: Script is built from real interviews creating an authentic, polyphonic narrative
Flexible casting—actors often portray multiple roles
Pivotal role in educational discussions about hate crimes and LGBTQ+ rights
Frequently produced on stages across America and internationally
Catalyst for public conversations about tolerance and equality
cultural_historical_context: Developed in response to the murder of gay student Matthew Shepard in Laramie, Wyoming in 1998, the play premiered in 2000 and was published in 2001. Its creation coincided with heightened national attention to LGBTQ+ rights, hate crime legislation, and debates about social inclusion. The play captures a specific historical moment when America grappled with its attitudes toward sexual orientation and violence.
reception_impact: Widely acclaimed for its emotional power, documentary authenticity, and social relevance
Used in educational and activist contexts to raise awareness of hate crimes
Inspired follow-up works, such as 'The Laramie Project: Ten Years Later'
Influenced legislation and contributed to the national dialogue on LGBTQ+ issues
Occasionally met with controversy or protest in conservative communities
comparable_titles: The Laramie Project: Ten Years Later by Moisés Kaufman and the Tectonic Theater Project
Angels in America by Tony Kushner
The Normal Heart by Larry Kramer
Our Town by Thornton Wilder (for its community focus and structure)
8 by Dustin Lance Black (another docudrama about LGBTQ+ legal issues)
